newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity ends down as traders take profit.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity ends down as traders take profit.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended lower Tuesday as players took profits following gains Monday and Tuesday morning on news of a California nuclear outage, industry sources said.
Palo Verde futures prices initially moved higher Tuesday morning, then backed off in profit taking, the sources said.
August Palo Verde (PV) finished down $1.36 at $33.54 per megawatt hour (MWh) after exchanges at $33.40-35.10, while September ended down 31 cents at $28.40 after exchanges at $28.00-28.60 per MWh.
Remaining PV deferreds finished down between 15 and 24 cents.
August California Oregon Border (COB) closed down 47 cents at $22.93 after trades at $22.60-23.30, while September settled down 49 cents at the $22.80-23.30 per MWh.
Remaining COB deferreds finished down 15 to 35 cents.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 347 COB and 790 PV contracts had traded.
The PV futures intially rose Tuesday on news the 1,070 megawatt (MW) San Onofre 2 nuclear unit in California would remain shut for a two week repair outage.
Southern California Edison Co said it expects San Onofre 2 to remain off line until July 15 to replace its charge line check valves.
The adjacent 1,080 MW San Onofre unit 3 also remained out of service for refueling, and was scheduled to resume operation around July 10.

Also, the 560 megawatt (MW) Agua Fria natural gas-fired power plant was shut late Monday, market sources said, adding the outage was not seen having a large impact on markets because it is considered to be a peaking unit.
The WNP-2 nuclear plant in Washington state was expected to stay down as it continued to await clearance from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission before beginning start-up operations.
A 550 MW unit at the coal-fired Laramie River Station in Wyoming was said to have tripped off line Sunday, with no restart date available.
The six to 10 day forecast called for temperatures in the Pacific Northwest to average below normal, while those in the Southwest would run above normal.
Late last week the Western Systems Coordinating Council board approved a derating of the Pacific Intertie transmission sytem to 6,300 MW from the current 7,200 MW, which was to be effective today.
